subject: Runtime path recommendation — hosted vs dedicated qualification
messages:
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.com>
To: Alyssa Chen <alyssa@quicksell.com>, Quicksell Ops <ops@quicksell.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 5 Nov 2026 15:08:00 -0800
Subject: Post-call recap + data request — latency/throughput for runtime recommendation

Hi Alyssa — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and the small set of items we need to validate the right deployment path (Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private VPC):

Summary from call:
- Primary feature: real-time price recommendations in checkout (sub-100ms soft targets).
- Expected steady-state: ~180–250 QPS during peak windows, spiky bursts to ~400 QPS for short intervals.
- Typical payload size: ~1.2–1.8 KB per request (mostly short contexts + user metadata).
- Tail latency sensitivity: p95/p99 are the key metrics rather than average.

What we need to make a concrete recommendation and pilot plan:
1) Historical QPS distribution (1h granularity if possible) for last 30 days — especially peak windows.
2) Measured p50/p95/p99 for your current model (if you have traces) for 3 sequence lengths: short/medium/long.
3) Concurrent request profile (how many parallel sessions during peak 95th percentile).
4) Any regulatory constraints (data residency, VPC requirement) or compliance needs.
5) Decision horizon: pilot -> prod timeline and any procurement constraints.

If you can drop the traces or a small sample into the Google Sheet we linked on the call, we’ll use that to run a realistic continuous-batching simulation and give you a clear cost/latency tradeoff.

Attachments: request_template.csv (a short template for the distribution table).

Next steps we propose:
- You: drop the QPS and trace sample (items 1–3) — target EOD Friday PT.
- Us: run a short bench (48–72h) and return: recommended runtime (Hosted pilot vs Dedicated reserved pool), estimated cost delta, and a proposed pilot config.
- If Dedicated is recommended, we’ll include a conservative capacity plan + warm-up steps.

Thanks — feel free to reply inline. If it’s easier we can spin up a quick call with our performance engineer.

Best,
Vivek Kulkarni
Enterprise Solutions
Redwood Inference

Thanks Vivek — appreciate the clear list. I uploaded the first-pass data and a small p95 trace bundle to the shared sheet and zipped traces (see links/attachments below). Key notes from our side:

- Steady-state QPS: 160–220 during US evening peaks (18:00–21:00 PT).
- Burst behavior: marketing pushes create 4–8 minute spikes to 380–420 QPS.
- Measured p95 (current infra): ~120ms, p99 ~220ms for the most common short-sequence workloads.
- Concurrency: typical concurrent sessions at peak ~35–45, but we occasionally see bounces to ~90 when multiple campaigns overlap.
- No strict data residency issues; we can accept US-only hosting. VPC is preferred for production but not mandatory for pilot.

Links/attachments:
- Google Sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1QkQuicksell-latency-qps
- Attachment: quicksell-p95-traces.zip (p95 traces + sample requests)

We’re aiming for a pilot in Q4 and a full rollout by end of Q1 if the numbers work out. Happy to set up the technical deep-dive next week.

Alyssa
Head of Product
Quicksell

Subject: Recommendation draft: pilot approach and quick sizing notes

Hi Alyssa — thanks for the uploads, the dataset was helpful. I ran a quick econometric check with our perf-sim (see attached pilot config) and wanted to share a pragmatic recommendation — written to minimize risk while meeting your p95 targets.

Short recommendation (pilot -> production):
- Pilot: Hosted API with a reserved burst plan + prefix caching for 2 weeks. Purpose: validate end-to-end integration quickly and measure real-world tail behavior under our continuous-batching runtime.
  - Why: Hosted lets us iterate on prompt caching strategies and model variants without procurement lead time. We can hit p95 ~80–120ms for short sequences in Hosted during normal peak traffic; bursts will degrade but are observable.
- Production (if SLA required): Move to Dedicated capacity (3x inference workers, autoscale buffer for burst up to 420 QPS) in your preferred region, with VPC peering if you opt for private networking.
  - Why: Dedicated gives predictable tail latency, consistent KV cache locality, and better isolation for predictable peaks. Our sims show a 20–30% reduction in p99 vs an unconstrained Hosted setup for your burst profile.

Estimated immediate asks for the pilot (action items):
1) Sign pilot SOW addendum (2-week hosted credit + engineering hours) — Ben, I’ll need you to draft the addendum template.
2) Schedule a 60-minute bench call next Tue with Quicksell devs + Redwood performance team to confirm payload shapes and warm-up sequences.
3) If you prefer to skip Hosted and go straight to Dedicated, we’ll need a 30-day commit for reserved GPUs to secure capacity (procurement & billing lead time).

Attachments: redwood-pilot-config.yaml (suggested batch sizes, kv-cache TTLs, model variants to try).

Cost note (very rough):
- Hosted pilot (2 weeks, burstable): low up-front cost using credits — good for validation.
- Dedicated 3-worker commit (monthly): higher baseline but lower per-token cost and more stable tail latency. We’ll provide a formal cost delta after the bench run.

Let us know which path you prefer. If you’d like, we can include a canary routing plan so you can start in Hosted and transparently fail over to Dedicated for high-volume windows.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
